security_spec.violation_condition: OpenSBI M-mode trap handler reads or writes mireg*/sireg* CSRs without first explicitly setting miselect/siselect to a validated value. Since these CSRs form an indirection window controlled by the select register, and the select value was last written by untrusted S-mode software before the trap, M-mode unwittingly accesses register state gated by an attacker-controlled index. An S-mode attacker sets miselect to an unimplemented or unexpected value, then invokes an SBI call—OpenSBI's handler accesses mireg* and triggers UNSPECIFIED behavior (hardware hang, spurious exception, or register state leak from a different select context).
security_spec.summary: Unvalidated miselect/siselect in M-mode trap handlers allows S-mode to control what register state M-mode observes through the indirect CSR window, enabling privilege escalation via UNSPECIFIED behavior on unimplemented select values

findings.finding: All four IMSIC indirect CSR access macros explicitly write CSR_MISELECT to a compile-time IMSIC constant (e.g., IMSIC_EITHRESHOLD, IMSIC_EIDELIVERY, IMSIC_EIP0..EIP63) before accessing CSR_MIREG. The miselect register is always overwritten with a trusted, validated value before each mireg read/write. Even when invoked from the SBI trap handler path (e.g., IPI processing), miselect is set first. No code path reads or writes mireg* without a preceding miselect write.

spec_citations.excerpt: The value of miselect determines which register is accessed upon read or write of each of the machine indirect alias CSRs (mireg*).
The behavior upon accessing mireg* from M-mode, while miselect holds a value that is not implemented, is UNSPECIFIED.

findings.finding: CSR_SIREG through CSR_SIREG6 are defined as constants but are never referenced in any .c or .S source file in the OpenSBI codebase. OpenSBI M-mode firmware does not access sireg* CSRs in any code path, including the trap handler, HSM suspend/resume, domain context switch, or platform init. No vulnerability exists because the CSRs are simply never accessed.

#define CSR_SIREG                 0x151
#define CSR_SIREG2                0x152
#define CSR_SIREG3                0x153
#define CSR_SIREG4                0x155
#define CSR_SIREG5                0x156
#define CSR_SIREG6                0x157

spec_citations.excerpt: The behavior upon accessing sireg* from M-mode or S-mode, while siselect holds a value that is not implemented at supervisor level, is UNSPECIFIED.

findings.finding: CSR_MIREG2 through CSR_MIREG6 are defined but never accessed by any code. Only CSR_MIREG (the primary alias) is used, exclusively via the IMSIC macros in imsic.c which set miselect first. The multi-register aliases (mireg2-6) for 64-bit indirect access are not needed by the IMSIC driver since all IMSIC registers accessed indirectly are XLEN-wide.

findings.finding: When Smcsrind is detected, the mstatus_init function correctly sets SMSTATEEN0_SVSLCT (bit 60) in mstateen0. Per the Smcsrind spec, this bit controls S-mode access to siselect/sireg*/vsiselect/vsireg*. Setting this bit before entering S-mode ensures S-mode software can use the indirect CSR access mechanism. When Smcsrind is not present, the bit is correctly cleared. The logic also correctly handles the SMAIA||SMCSRIND disjunction — the bit is needed when either extension (or both) is present.

spec_citations.excerpt: If extension Smstateen is implemented together with Smcsrind, bit 60 of state-enable register mstateen0 controls access to siselect, sireg*, vsiselect, and vsireg*. When mstateen0[60]=0, an attempt to access one of these CSRs from a privilege mode less privileged than M-mode results in an illegal-instruction exception.

findings.finding: The non-retentive suspend save path saves MIE, MIP, MEDELEG, MIDELEG, and MENVCFG but does NOT save miselect (or siselect). On resume, miselect resets to its hardware-default value. While all M-mode mireg accesses go through IMSIC macros that set miselect first, the loss of miselect state across suspend/resume means: (1) if the suspend occurred during a sequence where miselect was temporarily set to a non-default value, the resumed context is inconsistent; (2) siselect is not saved either, so S-mode's indirect CSR context is silently corrupted after non-retentive resume. This is a state-integrity gap, though not the specific trap-handler attack vector described in the vulnerability pattern.
